summary: Teach a/b as a ÷ b — the fraction bar means divide — by having learners share several wholes equally among more people than there are wholes. Sharing 3 bars among 4 children gives each 3/4, making 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4 a result learners produce and see, not a rule to memorise. Verify with the inverse (3/4 × 4 = 3) and extend to division with remainders expressed as mixed numbers (50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9, the leftover 5 shared among 9). Directly contrasting a÷b with b÷a keeps the direction of division meaningful.
misconceptions: 'You can't divide a smaller number by a larger one', so 3 ÷ 4 is declared impossible or flipped to 4 ÷ 3
Stops at a whole-number remainder ('5 remainder 5') instead of expressing it as 5 5/9
Treats 3/4 as only '3 out of 4 parts', unconnected to the division 3 ÷ 4

activities.title: Share the bars: discover 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4
steps: Set up the problem: 3 identical chocolate bars to share equally among 4 children.
BEFORE cutting, predict and give a reason: can everyone get the same, and if so how much each? Sit with the 'there aren't enough bars' feeling if it arises.
Cut each bar into 4 equal quarters.
Deal one quarter from every bar to each child, then count what ends up on each plate (3 quarters).
Write the result as a division: 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4.
Check in reverse: show that 3/4 × 4 rebuilds the 3 whole bars.
Compare directions: share 4 bars among 3 children and work out 4 ÷ 3 = 1 1/3; note that 3 ÷ 4 and 4 ÷ 3 give different answers.
activities.insight: A fraction a/b is exactly the quotient a ÷ b; you can divide a smaller number by a larger one and the answer is a fraction. The order of division matters, so 3 ÷ 4 ≠ 4 ÷ 3.

activities.title: Remainders are divisions too: 50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9
steps: Pose: 9 people share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight — how many pounds each?
Give out whole pounds first: 5 each uses 45 pounds, leaving 5 pounds.
Decide what to do with the leftover 5 pounds: share those 5 among the 9 people too.
Express that leftover share as a fraction: 5 ÷ 9 = 5/9.
Combine to the mixed number: 5 5/9 pounds each.
Sanity-check the size: the answer lies between 5 and 6.
activities.insight: A whole-number division with a remainder has an exact answer as a mixed number; the remainder is itself a division (the leftover shared among the same group).

activities.title: Check and discriminate: name the division and verify
steps: Given a sharing situation (e.g. 3 bars among 4 children), state how much each gets AND which division it represents.
Explain how to check the answer using inverse multiplication (3/4 × 4 = 3).

Answer a short set of linked items: 3 ÷ 4 = ? (compare against the tempting wrong answers 1 1/3 (which comes from working out 4 ÷ 3 instead) and 'impossible', both labelled as incorrect answers to 3 ÷ 4); fill in 50 ÷ 9 = 5 __/9; match each division to its fraction or mixed-number result.
Say in your own words why a share of 3 bars among 4 is less than one whole each.
activities.insight: Being able to name 3/4 as 3 ÷ 4 and verify it with ×4 — not just read it as 'three out of four parts' — is what shows the division meaning has been grasped.

checkQuestion: Here are 3 identical chocolate bars to share equally among 4 children. How much does each child get? Then tell me: what division does this sharing represent, and how could you check your answer is right?
checkAnswer: Each child gets 3/4 of a bar. This represents 3 ÷ 4 (the fraction bar means divide), and it checks because 3/4 × 4 = 3 — the three original bars.
